title: The $9.5 Billion Design IP Market: Shifting Boundaries, Arm’s Monopoly, and the RISC-V Response - Semiwiki
gist: The 2025 design-IP market grew 12.7% to $9.45B, with Arm consolidating a near-monopoly (93.3% of CPU IP) while pushing into its own silicon (AGI chips), triggering a 'co-opetition crisis' that is fueling explosive growth for RISC-V specialists like SiFive, Syntacore and Semidynamics, even as Synopsys divests its CPU IP business to GlobalFoundries and budgets pivot toward security and system IP.

insights.claim: The worldwide design IP market grew 12.7% in 2025 to reach $9,451.9 million, according to the SemiWiki Design IP Report.
insights.speaker: Kalar Rajendiran
insights.so_what: Double-digit IP market growth in a mixed macro environment confirms IP licensing revenue as a resilient, high-visibility proxy for downstream chip design activity.

insights.claim: Design IP functions as the architectural bottleneck for the entire global semiconductor value chain, with choices made at the IP layer today dictating the cost, power and security of a technology economy the author expects to approach a trillion dollars by decade's end.
insights.speaker: Kalar Rajendiran
insights.so_what: Investors should treat IP vendor share shifts as leading indicators for downstream cost/power/security outcomes across the entire chip industry, not just a niche licensing line item.

insights.claim: CPU IP and Wired Interface IP together account for 69% of total design IP spend across the market's 12 sub-categories.
insights.speaker: Kalar Rajendiran
insights.so_what: Concentration in two categories means competitive dynamics there (Arm's dominance, interconnect standards battles) disproportionately drive overall market economics.

insights.claim: Royalty revenue surged 16.1% versus a steadier 10.7% licensing growth, a divergence attributed to a wave of historical design wins completing the multi-year design-to-tape-out pipeline and entering high-volume wafer manufacturing.
insights.speaker: Kalar Rajendiran
insights.so_what: Faster royalty growth than licensing growth is a lagging confirmation that prior design-win cycles are now converting into real production volume -- a useful cross-check for foundry utilization trends.

themes.theme: Arm's CPU monopoly and the co-opetition crisis

insights.claim: Processor IP represents 52.2% of total design IP spend, and within it Arm grew 26.4% to capture 49.4% of the overall design IP market and 93.3% of the CPU IP market specifically.
insights.speaker: Kalar Rajendiran
insights.so_what: Arm's near-total CPU IP monopoly (93.3%) is a structural chokepoint risk for every licensee reliant on its architecture, and a key reason RISC-V alternatives are gaining urgency.

insights.claim: Arm's expansion into its own physical silicon production via Arm General Infrastructure (AGI) chips has created a 'co-opetition crisis': licensees whose primary CPU architecture partner is also becoming a direct competitor in infrastructure hardware.
insights.speaker: Kalar Rajendiran
insights.so_what: Cloud hyperscalers and infrastructure providers licensing Arm cores now face a strategic conflict of interest with their IP supplier, increasing incentive to hedge with alternative architectures -- watch for accelerated RISC-V adoption among Arm's largest customers.

insights.claim: The Arm co-opetition anxiety is driving an aggressive industry push toward architectural autonomy via the open-standard RISC-V architecture, though the market response is highly polarized between high-growth specialists and contracting incumbents.
insights.speaker: Kalar Rajendiran
insights.so_what: RISC-V's growth is explicitly framed as a defensive hedge against Arm concentration risk, not merely a cost play -- a structural tailwind for RISC-V core vendors independent of near-term macro conditions.

insights.claim: Dedicated RISC-V specialists posted explosive growth in 2025: SiFive's CPU IP revenue surged 34.6%, Syntacore grew 35.3%, and Semidynamics grew 22.2%.
insights.speaker: Kalar Rajendiran
insights.so_what: These specific growth rates identify the RISC-V vendors best positioned to capture share from Arm-hedging chipmakers; useful as a screen for private/strategic investment interest.

insights.claim: Synopsys' CPU IP revenue declined 27.3% following its 2026 strategic divestment of the CPU IP business to GlobalFoundries, while RISC-V pioneer Andes Technology saw a minor 6.2% slide tied to licensing-contract timing rather than a long-term trend.
insights.speaker: Kalar Rajendiran
insights.so_what: Synopsys' exit from CPU IP into GlobalFoundries' hands signals reshuffling of foundry-vs-EDA-vendor boundaries around processor IP ownership -- a notable consolidation event to track for competitive realignment.

insights.claim: Year-over-year CPU IP performance among established RISC-V and Arm-adjacent vendors is heavily tied to the timing of major licensing contract milestones rather than reflecting genuine long-term market trends.
insights.speaker: Kalar Rajendiran
insights.so_what: Investors should discount single-year CPU IP revenue swings at mid-tier vendors and instead track multi-year design-win pipelines before drawing conclusions about competitive position.

themes.theme: Budget pivot: security and interconnects over standard cells

insights.claim: Security IP grew 22.5% and System IP grew 22.2% in 2025, while Physical Library (Standard Cell & I/O) IP contracted 4.6%, even though overall design IP growth was 12.7%.
insights.speaker: Kalar Rajendiran
insights.so_what: As AI workloads migrate to the edge and data centers demand secure, high-bandwidth interconnects, design budgets are visibly reallocating toward hardware-level trust and SoC fabric at the expense of commoditized standard-cell licensing -- a signal for where IP vendor pricing power will concentrate.

insights.claim: Arm, Synopsys (18.5% share) and Cadence (6.4% share) together control 74.4% of the global design IP market, leaving a fierce competitive war among mid-tier vendors for the remaining share in high-speed interface, custom analog, and non-volatile memory niches.
insights.speaker: Kalar Rajendiran
insights.so_what: With 74.4% concentrated among three vendors, the remaining ~25.6% mid-tier market is where differentiated M&A targets and share-gain stories are most likely to emerge.

insights.claim: Some specialty mid-tier IP vendors rode system, security, and mixed-signal analog demand to explosive double-digit growth in 2025, while others hit unexpected revenue plateaus as legacy-node demand contracted.
insights.speaker: Kalar Rajendiran
insights.so_what: Mid-tier IP vendor performance is bifurcating sharply by end-market exposure -- distinguishing winners exposed to security/analog/system IP from losers tied to legacy nodes is key competitive intelligence.
